chunks: He said: Abu Ubaydullah Muhammad ibn Imran al-Marzbani reported to me from Abdullah ibn Yahya al-Askari, who reported from Ahmad ibn Zayd ibn Ahmad, who reported from Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Aktham Abu Abdillah, who reported from his father Yahya ibn Aktham al-Maruzi, who said:

Al-Ma'mun summoned Du'bal ibn Ali al-Khuza'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and granted him safe conduct. When he arrived before him, and I was sitting near al-Ma'mun, he said to him: 'Recite to me your great poem.' Du'bal denied it and disclaimed knowing it. So al-Ma'mun said: 'You have safety for it, just as I granted you safety for yourself.' So Du'bal recited to him:

[Du'bal's poem, part 1:] My wife regretted when she saw my indifference, and considered my maturity a sin unforgivable. She expects youthfulness after her forelocks turned grey, though she has already run a round in the arena of old age. O wife, my hoary head teaches me to remember the Resurrection and to submit to destiny. Had I been inclined to the world and its adornment, I would have wept over some who have passed. Time attacked my family and shattered them like a tribe hit by a stone. Some remained, some answered the call of death, and the rest follow on their trail. I fear the departure of those who stay, and the return of the departed is not awaited. I am told about my family and children like a dreamer relating a dream after remembering. Were it not that my eyes are preoccupied with those who passed from the family of the Messenger of Allah, I would not have found rest. Your cheeks are occupied weeping for your friends, unable to sleep because of the lost ones. How many arms lie severed at Karbala, and cheeks covered in dust on the plain! They went to where al-Husayn was slain, saying: 'This is the master of mankind.' O ungrateful nation! You did not reward Ahmad for his struggle for the Revelation and the Chapters. When he passed, you treated his children as a wolf would treat cattle.
Yahya said: Then al-Ma'mun sent me on an errand. I went and when I returned, Du'bal had reached the following verse:

[Du'bal's poem, part 2:] There remains no living soul we know, from the tribes of Yemen, Bakr or Mudhar, except that they have a share in their blood, as did the participants in the slaughter. By killing, capturing, terrorizing, and plundering, the way soldiers acted in the lands of Byzantines and Khazars. I find the Umayyads excused if they killed, but I find no excuse for the sons of al-Abbas! A people you first killed in the name of Islam, then when you seized power, you surpassed in disbelief. Sons of Harb, Marwan, and their families, the sons of Mu'ayt, rulers of rancour and spite. Pause at Tus upon the grave of the pure one, if you hold on to anything of faith! Alas! Every person is mortgaged by what his two hands earned, so take what you wish or leave it.
He said: So al-Ma'mun threw his turban on the ground and said: 'You have spoken the truth, by Allah, O Du'bal.'

key_terms.الزكي: The Pure One -- reference to Imam al-Ridha
key_terms.الطف: Karbala -- the plain where Imam al-Husayn was martyred
key_terms.بطوس: At Tus -- city where Imam al-Ridha is buried
key_terms.دعبل: Du'bal ibn Ali al-Khuza'i -- famous Shia poet (d. 246 AH)

ai.seo_question: What is the famous poem Du'bal recited before Caliph al-Ma'mun about the Ahl al-Bayt?
ai.summary: Yahya ibn Aktham, the chief judge of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun, narrates how the caliph summoned the famous Shia poet Du'bal ibn Ali al-Khuza'i and, after granting him safe conduct, asked him to recite his famous qasida. Du'bal's poem mourns the persecution of the Ahl al-Bayt, laments the tragedy of Karbala, condemns both the Umayyads and Abbasids for their crimes against the Prophet's family, and mentions the grave of the pure one (Imam al-Ridha) at Tus. Upon hearing the verse, al-Ma'mun was so moved that he threw his turban on the ground and exclaimed: 'By Allah, you have spoken the truth, O Du'bal.'
word_analysis: may He have mercy on him
